title: Income, Wealth, and Poverty
question: Why do some people have much more than others, and what should the country do about poverty?
summary: Living standards, what “poor” means in the statistics, and the argument over inequality. Definitions first, numbers only after they are checked.
sourceNote: Further reading only. This outline does not take facts from these pages yet. When the full page is written, government or other primary sources will be cited first, and the Just Facts page will stay linked as further reading. The wording on this site will stay original. No statistics are included here.

paragraphs: This section will explain the difference between income (money coming in) and wealth (what someone owns minus what they owe), and why a poverty line is a definition people argue about rather than a fact of nature.
No statistics will be added until they are checked against primary sources.

This section will name the disagreement over whether a wide gap is mostly a story about effort and growth or mostly a story about unfair rules. It will not treat “the rich have more” as the end of the argument, because both sides already know that.

sides.intro: Each column will hold one side’s strongest fair case, in plain language and at similar length. Neither case is written yet.

a.title: One side’s strongest case
paragraphs: This column will give the strongest fair case for one view, using checked facts. It will not use insults, and it is not written yet.

b.title: The other side’s strongest case
paragraphs: This column will give the strongest fair case for the other view, under the same rules. It is not written yet.
This section will look for shared concerns, such as wanting people to be able to afford food and housing, and wanting a measure of poverty that does not hide how people actually live.

items: The questions will ask what a fair starting point would look like, what a statistic leaves out, and whether a rising average can still leave people behind.

sources.title: U.S. Census Bureau: Income and Poverty
